author: pro.glitch
caption: Build a second brain with Claude You save the article. You write the meeting notes. You keep the customer email. Three weeks later you can't find any of it. Here's the second brain I'd build instead. Three pieces: A folder of plain text files on your computer. You own it. Obsidian opens the folder and shows the files and the links between them as a map. That's where you read. Claude Code opens the same folder and does all the writing. Inside the folder: raw (everything you drop in, never edited), wiki (pages Claude writes and keeps current, each linking back to its sources) and CLAUDE.md (the rulebook). Three jobs. Ingest: drop in Monday's call notes and one call updates five pages. Ask: every answer points to the raw note it came from. Lint: once a week the brain checks itself for pages that disagree, orphan pages and numbers with no source. The rules that stop the confident nonsense: no source, no number. Every claim tagged as extracted or inferred. Little data means "early signal", not fact. Old claims get marked outdated, never deleted. Start with one client, one project, or your own business. #claudecode #aiautomation #aiagents #aiemployee

author: paytonkaleiwahea
caption: The one prompt edit with Claude, step by step. No DM for resources, it's all right here. 1. Install Claude Code (Codex works too). Download the desktop app. 2. Open Claude Code. It opens in Chat, so switch it over to Code. 3. Make a folder on your computer. Mine is called My Boss Editor. 4. Select the folder: Local, then Open folder. That's your workspace. 5. Copy these GitHub repositories: • FFmpeg: every cut, crop, mix, mute and render · github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg • faster-whisper: word-level transcription every cut is placed against · github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper • Whisper: OpenAI's speech model that faster-whisper runs · github.com/openai/whisper • yt-dlp: downloads the source video · github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp • OpenCV + contrib: follows whoever is talking in the vertical crop · github.com/opencv/opencv and github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib • Puppeteer: headless Chrome that renders the captions and titles to video · github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer • HyperFrames: agent-built motion graphics from HTML · github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes 6. Prompt Claude and give it the links: "You are my short form editor. Here are all the GitHub links to help you do your job." 7. Find an edit you like and send it: "I like the style of this reel. Can we duplicate this style and use it for a video of mine?" 8. Shoot your video. 9. Send it to Claude. Copy the path of the file and paste it in. 10. Review it and use your voice to edit. Bonus: turn it into a skill. "Hey, turn this into a skill." Next time it knows the process. This was not me going into a timeline. Claude edited it in the same list style as the reel I sent it. I know it is a lot, but that's also probably why they're selling their courses. #claudecode #aivideoediting #videoediting #contentcreator #ai

author: webloved
caption: How I build with Claude 👇 Academy in bio 🔗 Full prompt goes in the Academy soon. It took hours of testing to get right. Want a site like this? Send me an email, email in bio 📩 One product, three flavours. Let the whole page change colour as you scroll into each one: 1. Give each flavour section an id: cacao, peche, framboise. 2. One palette per flavour as CSS variables: :root[data-flavour="cacao"] { --bg: rgb(243,232,222); --ink: rgb(74,44,30) }. Same for the other two. 3. IntersectionObserver with rootMargin "-50% 0px -50% 0px", so it fires when a section crosses the middle of the screen. 4. On fire, set document.documentElement.dataset.flavour to that id. 5. body gets transition: background-color 600ms, color 600ms. The page melts from one flavour to the next. 6. 6 to 8 ingredient PNGs per flavour, each moving at its own speed: 0.2 to 0.6 times the scroll. 7. Small ones slower with filter: blur(2px), big ones faster and sharp. Instant depth, no WebGL. 8. The Add to bag button uses --ink too, so the button always matches the flavour on screen. Save this before your next product site 🔥 #claude #claudeai #webdesign #vibecoding #3dwebsite

author: meycuanc
caption: Parte 2: cómo crear tu Design System en Claude 💻 Si ya hiciste tu branding en ChatGPT, ahora toca convertirlo en reglas para que tus carruseles, presentaciones y diseños no parezcan de marcas diferentes cada vez 😭 Paso 1. Pídele a ChatGPT un resumen de tu marca: “Hazme un resumen de mi marca con qué hace, para quién es, personalidad, tono, colores, tipografías, estilo visual y qué cosas debe evitar. No inventes nada nuevo; usa únicamente lo que ya construimos.” Paso 2. Descarga tu moodboard. Paso 3. Guarda 3–5 referencias de carruseles o diseños que representen el estilo que quieres conseguir. No es para copiarlos. Son para que Claude entienda cosas como composición, jerarquías, tamaño de títulos, uso de fotos, cantidad de texto, etc. Paso 4. Sube a Claude: • resumen de marca • moodboard • referencias de diseño Y usa este prompt: “Voy a darte tres cosas: un resumen escrito de mi marca, un moodboard visual y varios ejemplos de carruseles y diseños cuyo estilo me gusta. Quiero que uses el resumen para entender la personalidad, público, propósito, tono y valores de la marca. Usa el moodboard para entender la identidad visual ya definida: colores, tipografías, logo, estilo, dirección visual y sensación general. Y usa los ejemplos de carruseles y diseños para entender cómo quiero que esa identidad se vea aplicada en piezas reales: composición, jerarquía, distribución, ritmo, uso de imágenes, cantidad de texto y estilo de cada slide. No copies literalmente los diseños de referencia y no inventes una nueva identidad. A partir de todo esto, crea un Design System completo para mi marca. author: kodekloud
caption: Why Git Wasn’t Enough for Anthropic!! Anthropic’s AI agents merge over 30,000 code updates every single day, triggering a staggering 25 million automated testing jobs. Under standard Git, every single test machine had to clone gigabytes of repository history just to verify a one-file bug fix, generating an unsustainable 600 petabytes of network traffic daily. Because Git was designed decades ago for offline human developers who download an entire codebase to their local laptops, it completely buckled under the rapid-fire demands of automated AI development. To eliminate this bottleneck, Anthropic built Scion, a custom version control system where full code history stays on central servers while test runners fetch only the exact folder they need. Using content-based file IDs paired with smart multi-tier caching, Scion answers over 99% of file requests instantly, slashing checkout times from minutes to seconds and saving 25% of testing CPU power. Incredibly, a tiny team of just seven engineers built the entire replacement system using Claude in only five months. #SystemDesign #Anthropic #DevOps #SoftwareEngineering #AIEngineering #TechNews

author: webloved
caption: How I build with Claude 👇 Academy in bio 🔗 Full prompt goes in the Academy soon. It took hours of testing to get right. Want a site like this? Send me an email, email in bio 📩 This site feels like one shot, not 5 sections. The trick is match cuts: every section ends on what the next one starts with: 1. Plan the page as one story: beans, grind, pour, drop, cup, shop. 2. The hero object sits at the exact same spot in every section: left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%). The eye never jumps. 3. One thread ties it all together: the falling stream. A 4px div fixed in the centre, transform: scaleY(progress), transform-origin: top. 4. Make every image with the same angle and light. Add "centered, 85mm, soft side light, same background" to each prompt, or the cut breaks. 5. Crossfade sections over the last 20% of each one with opacity, so the cup already shows before the drop is gone. 6. One data line per step, like 92°C, 18g, 3:29. Numbers make it read as craft, not decoration. 7. End on product cards that reuse the frames from the journey as thumbnails. The shop is the last scene, not a new page. 8. author: presailapp
caption: Presailapp.com #creatorsearchinsights #smallcontentcreators #vibecoding #app #newaccountontiktok  Presail AI is a security platform designed to help developers, founders, and entrepreneurs identify potential vulnerabilities in their applications before those weaknesses become serious problems. As AI-powered coding platforms such as Base44, Lovable, Bolt, and other vibe-coding tools make it easier than ever to build and launch software without extensive programming experience, more people are publishing applications without necessarily understanding the security risks behind them. Presail aims to address this problem by making application security more accessible, understandable, and actionable, especially for indie hackers, SaaS founders, startups, and nontechnical builders who want to launch confidently without needing to become cybersecurity experts. Instead of expecting users to manually inspect code, understand complicated security terminology, or hire expensive security professionals for every early-stage project, Presail provides a streamlined experience in which users can submit or scan their applications, receive an analysis of potential security issues, and understand what those findings could mean for their product and its users. The platform’s goal is not simply to display a list of technical warnings, but to help developers understand which issues deserve attention, why they matter, and what steps they can take to address them. Security problems can include improperly exposed secrets, insecure access controls, weaknesses in authentication, potentially vulnerable application logic, misconfigured permissions, and other issues that could put sensitive information or application functionality at risk, depending on what the platform’s scanning capabilities support. Presail is being developed around the idea that security should be considered before an application gains users, collects sensitive information, or becomes a real business, rather than treated as an afterthought once something goes wrong. Its intended value is especially relevant to people who move quickly from idea to prototype to launch and may not have a dedicated security team to review their work. By combining a straightforward interface, an approachable scanning experience, and useful explanations of findings, Presail aims to make security testing feel less intimidating and more practical for everyday builders. The broader vision is to become a trusted security companion for the growing ecosystem of AI-assisted software development, helping independent creators and growing companies make more informed decisions about the applications they build and publish. Presail is not intended to replace a comprehensive professional penetration test, a qualified security engineer, or every other layer of a mature security program; rather, its purpose is to make identifying and understanding potential security weaknesses more accessible during development and before launch. Ultimately, Presail AI is built around one core belief: building software has become dramatically easier, but making sure that software is secure still matters just as much. By helping close the gap between rapid application development and security awareness, Presail aims to give developers a clearer path toward building, improving, and launching software with greater confidence.

author: legitalgorithmswithpeter
caption: Vibe Coding vs Real Software Engineering 🤖💻 The debate isn’t “AI writes bad code.” It’s that AI can write code that looks correct while violating the actual intent. LLMs predict plausible tokens — they don’t verify business logic, security, concurrency, or correctness. That creates risks like: 📦 Package hallucination → AI recommends packages that don’t exist. ☠️ Slopsquatting → Attackers register those names and publish malicious packages. And the senior vs junior gap matters. A senior engineer can spot a broken authorization check or race condition because they’ve seen similar failures before. A junior may not have that mental library yet — making AI confidence look like correctness. The same problem appears during debugging: if you didn’t design the code, you first have to reconstruct why it exists before figuring out why it broke. Vibe coding makes sense for prototypes and low-stakes tools. But production systems still need architecture, review, testing, and verification. And teams are increasingly using property-based testing and fuzzing to test generated code across huge input spaces. The real question: If AI writes the code juniors used to learn from, where does the next generation of senior engineers come from? 👀 #VibeCoding #AIProgramming #SoftwareEngineering #AIEngineering #DeveloperSkills

author: jbatten_builds
caption: If you’re trying to get into vibecoding, please don’t let these tools trick you into thinking you don’t need a brain anymore 😂 For me, the two tools I recommend starting with are Cursor and Antigravity. 	•	Cursor is just a straight-up beast. I have not met an AI dev tool that really tops it yet. 	•	Antigravity is newer, fun, and the way it organizes files is actually clutch for new vibecoders who get overwhelmed by messy projects. But real talk: it does not matter what tool you start with if your back end is chaos. Before you get cute on the front end, you need to know: 	•	What are you using for auth? 	•	What are you using for your database? 	•	What’s your actual back-end stack? 	•	How are you going to deploy this thing? If you fuck up the back end, it truly won’t matter how pretty your UI is. As vibecoders, we already have a ton of knowledge gaps, and you cannot outsource that to AI. If every single prompt you send is full of words, tools, and dependencies you don’t understand, that’s your sign to stop prompting and go learn. The agent is not “thinking with you,” it’s just blindly implementing. You’re building a house on mud and vibes. 🧠 Slow down to speed up. Also: get your naming together. File names, function names, API names, folders — all that. If your shit is called test2-final-FINAL.js and newnewnew-api-fixed.js, you’re going to suffer later. And AI agents will too. If they can’t find the real file, they WILL make one up, and now you have duplicates, broken paths, and confusion on top of confusion. As a vibecoder, part of your “job” is: 	•	Doing cleanup days 	•	Fixing defects 	•	Organizing files 	•	Writing or updating docs Because once these agents get in your repo, they touch everything whether you meant for them to or not. This shit is powerful, but it’s not magic. You are still the engineer of record, even if the code came from an AI. 👇🏾 Are you vibecoding right now? What tools are you using—Cursor, Antigravity, Claude, Gemini, straight ChatGPT? And be honest: do you actually know what your back end is running on, or are you just hoping it doesn’t crash?  #swe #vibecoder #cursor #antigravity #opus

author: invokedynamics
caption: Vibecoder vs Real Coder #larp #vibecoder #code #coder A vibe coder is someone who builds software, apps, or websites by using natural language prompts to direct artificial intelligence rather than writing code manually. How Vibe Coding Works • Intent-Driven Development: Instead of typing syntax line-by-line, the creator tells an AI what they want in plain English (e.g., "Build a budgeting app with a login system"). • The AI Loop: The AI generates the code, structure, and database, and the user tests the output, spots errors, and feeds the feedback back into the model until the app works. • "Forgetting the Code": Coined by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in early 2025, the term describes a style where the builder completely detaches from the underlying source code, focusing only on the "vibe" and final user experience.

caption: What’s valuable in software engineering? Is it the code? The binary? No! It’s the specification! We can recreate the code from the specs - but it’s hard to recreate specs from code (just as it is hard to create readable nicely commented source code from a binary).  So why do we treat our source code as gold, but happily throw away user stories and other specifications?  And when coding with an AI like cursor.ai, we discard the conversations that specified the domain and just keep the code. That feels as stupid as throwing away the source code after we have compiled a binary from it! So: Treat your specs like code. Version them, structure and modularize them. author: umeladenne
caption: AI pracovala sedem dní sama. Nikto jej medzitým nehovoril, čo má robiť ďalej. Firma Cursor, ktorá robí nástroj na programovanie s umelou inteligenciou, dala svojim AI agentom jednu veľkú úlohu. Napísať internetový prehliadač, teda program, cez ktorý chodíš na internet. A potom ich nechala bežať takmer celý týždeň. Zaujímavé na tom nie je ani tak to, čo z toho vzniklo, ale ako to vznikalo. Agenti si sami rozplánovali prácu, písali kód, spúšťali testy, našli chyby a opravovali ich. Človek nezasahoval takmer vôbec. Za ten čas napísali vyše milióna riadkov kódu v tisícke súborov. To video hore je záznam tej práce. Každý bod je jeden súbor a vidíš, ako projekt rastie hodinu po hodine. Doteraz AI dobre zvládala krátke úlohy. Napíš mi text, oprav mi túto funkciu, zhrň mi tento dokument. Toto je iná liga. Týždeň znamená, že si systém musí pamätať, čo robil v pondelok, keď je piatok, a nestratiť pritom smer. Férovo treba dodať aj druhú stranu. Prehliadač zatiaľ nefunguje tak, ako má, a vývojári, ktorí si ho stiahli, hlásia chyby pri spúšťaní. Šéf firmy sám povedal, že to “akosi” funguje a že k použiteľnému prehliadaču má ďaleko. A nebol to jeden agent, ako sa píše na sieťach, ale stovky naraz. Ale otázka, ktorú ten experiment otvára, nie je o prehliadači. Je o tom, či sa práca časom nezmení tak, že človek bude určovať smer a vykonávať to budú agenti. Čo myslíš, koľko to potrvá? Napíš do komentárov. Zdroje: Cursor, GIGAZINE, 36Kr #ai #umelainteligencia #cursor #aiagent

author: picklerickursion
caption: Are you still paying $10 just to read the second half of a coding tutorial? 🧠 You are falling for a "client-side illusion." Rick shows Morty how to use the Developer Tools to disable JavaScript and remove the digital cardboard blocking the text that's already sitting in your RAM. Stop renting the internet and start owning it. (Plus, knowing simple tricks like this is exactly how you start building a massive faceless tech audience). 🚀 Deep Dive Description The Illusion: Many news sites and tutorial blogs use "Soft Paywalls." Instead of keeping the article on their secure server, they send the entire text to your browser, and then use a simple JavaScript code to trigger a popup overlay that hides it. The DevTools Hack:You don't need a credit card to bypass a client-side block; you just need to turn off the script doing the hiding. Press F12 to open Developer Tools. Press Ctrl + Shift + P to open the Command Menu. Type Disable JavaScript and hit Enter. Refresh the page. The popup will fail to load, leaving the raw text fully readable. The Catch: Modern web apps (like Twitter, YouTube, or Discord) rely entirely on JavaScript to function. If you leave it disabled, the modern internet will break and look like a blank page from 1995. You must repeat the steps and type Enable JavaScript when you are done reading. The Creator Pivot: You already know how to code, cook, or troubleshoot. If you screen-record simple solutions like this without ever showing your face, you can turn your basic competence into a highly monetized digital asset. Teach what you know. author: rick.theengineer
caption: Most teams don't break production because they're bad at code. They break it because a human had to remember every step. SSH into the server. Pull the latest code. Install. Build. Copy files. Restart. Hope nothing breaks. Forget one step, like the database migration, and the site goes down with a 502 error. That's the problem CI/CD solves. It has two halves: CI (Continuous Integration) answers one question: is this code safe to merge? Every push runs the same pipeline automatically. It installs dependencies, runs the linter, runs unit and integration tests, builds the app and scans for vulnerabilities. If one check fails, the pipeline turns red and that code can't be merged until it's fixed. CD answers a different question: can we safely release it? The tested code becomes a release artifact (often a Docker image). It goes to staging first, where more checks run, and then on to production. Here's the part most people mix up: → Continuous DELIVERY: a human still clicks "deploy" before production. → Continuous DEPLOYMENT: if every check passes, it ships automatically. No human needed. And when something still goes wrong, good pipelines don't just ask "did the server start?" They ask "are health checks passing?" They roll out to 5% of users first (a canary), then 25%, 50%, 100%, and they roll back the moment error rates spike. Everything in this video comes from a real run: real commits, real test results, a real failing test (expected $3.56, got $4), and a real GitHub Actions workflow file. The real point of CI/CD isn't speed. It's that every release follows the exact same steps, every single time. Watch it to the end: the bug that brings production down at the end is the step that got forgotten at the start 👀 Save this for your next system design interview, and send it to the friend who still deploys over SSH. Which side does your team run: delivery or deployment? 👇 #cicd #devops #githubactions #softwareengineering #coding

author: rick.theengineer
caption: Every time you hit send on WhatsApp, your message goes on a journey most people never see. 👀 Here's the whole backend roadmap in under 3 minutes, built from scratch, one stop at a time: 01 → Server: your app has to run somewhere (Java, Go, Python, JavaScript…) 02 → API: the contract your phone uses to talk to the server (POST /messages) 03 → Database: where your messages actually live (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB) 04 → Cache: Redis keeps hot data in memory so millions of users don't melt your database 05 → WebSockets: one open connection, so messages arrive in real time 06 → Message Queue: the sender doesn't wait while a background worker sends the push notification 07 → Load Balancer: one server isn't enough, so traffic gets spread across many 08 → Containers: Docker packages your app, Kubernetes runs it across machines 09 → Architecture: monolith vs microservices (spoiler: microservices aren't automatically better) 10 → Observability: metrics, logs and traces show what's really happening inside The big lesson: backend engineering isn't just writing endpoints. It's designing systems that stay secure, reliable and fast when millions of people use them. Watch it twice. author: kodekloud
caption: How DNS Works Step by Step Many people assume DNS is a single massive database containing every website's IP address, but it is actually a global distributed hierarchy. When you type google.com, your computer first checks your browser's cache and your operating system's shared cache. If neither knows the address, your computer asks a recursive resolver provided by your internet provider. To locate an unknown domain, this resolver queries the Root servers at the top of the internet, which point it to the servers running the .com registry, which then redirect the request directly to Google's authoritative name server. Google's authoritative server holds the official records and hands back the exact IP address, allowing your browser to finally start its connection. Although querying multiple servers for a single website sounds slow, aggressive caching at every single layer ensures your resolver rarely needs to start from the top, resolving most web lookups in just a few milliseconds. author: kodekloud
caption: Interview: How Browser Cookies Actually Work When you sign into a website like Apple and close your browser, you stay logged in because of browser cookies. During login, the server generates a unique session ID in its database and delivers it to your browser inside an HTTP Set-Cookie response header. A cookie is simply a small piece of text containing a key and value, guarded by strict browser directives like Secure to enforce encrypted HTTPS transmission and HttpOnly to stop malicious scripts from stealing your session token. On your next visit, your browser automatically attaches this saved cookie to your request, allowing the server to recognize your account and shopping cart instantly without asking for your password again. Cookies become controversial when third-party advertising networks use them to follow you across the internet. When an external ad provider loads banners across thousands of unrelated websites, it reads the same third-party tracking cookie to assemble a detailed profile of your browsing habits. This widespread tracking is why privacy regulations like GDPR force websites to show consent banners for marketing trackers, even while essential login cookies quietly do their job in the background. While attackers can impersonate you if they steal an active session cookie, these tiny text files remain the indispensable glue that keeps your daily digital life connected. #WebDevelopment #CyberSecurity #SoftwareEngineering #TechExplained #SystemDesign #CodingForBeginners

author: legitalgorithmswithpeter
caption: 💀 One wrong command deleted 300GB of production data. And EVERY backup had failed. This actually happened to GitLab in 2017. 🤯 An engineer was trying to fix a broken database replica. After hours of troubleshooting, he ran a command to wipe the data directory. But he was on the WRONG server. The live production database was gone. And then things got even worse. 🚨 💾 Cloud backups? Broken because of incompatible PostgreSQL tools. 📧 Warning emails? Never delivered. 🖥️ Disk snapshots? Not enabled for the database servers. 🔄 Database replica? Already wiped. GitLab had multiple backup strategies, but none could reliably save them. Then, pure luck saved the day. An engineer had copied a recent database snapshot to a staging server just hours earlier. GitLab recovered, but around six hours of database activity was permanently lost. 🔥 The biggest lesson? A backup you have never tested restoring isn’t a backup. author: jam.with.ai
caption: System design has many terms that sound similar… …but they solve very different problems. Here’s the simplest breakdown worth saving: LATENCY How long does one request take? THROUGHPUT How many requests can the system process over time? BANDWIDTH How much data can move through the network at once? — REPLICATION Copies the same data across multiple machines. SHARDING Splits different parts of the data across multiple machines. — POLLING Keeps asking: “Has anything changed?” WEBHOOK Automatically sends a notification when something happens. — PROCESS An independent program with its own memory. THREAD A smaller execution unit that shares memory within a process. — LOAD BALANCER Distributes traffic across multiple servers. API GATEWAY Controls how clients access APIs. — CONCURRENCY Handles multiple tasks during the same period. PARALLELISM Executes multiple tasks at exactly the same time. — MONOLITH Built and deployed as one complete application. MICROSERVICES Split into smaller services that can be developed and deployed independently. Small differences. Big impact when designing production systems. Save this for your system design and AI engineering interviews. . . . author: webloved
caption: How I build with Lovable 👇 Academy in bio 🔗 Every section of this site is the same forty-five thousand particles. Nothing else was ever added. The substitution, free. Bad: "cosmic design studio site, particle effects, stunning WebGL animations for each section" Good: "One particle system, forty-five thousand points, exists for the entire site. It never resets. Each section only reshapes it: sphere, then star, then crater, then comet, then spiral. No section introduces a new visual element. The last shape becomes the contact form." Beginners give every section its own idea. That is why their sites feel like five sites stapled together. A year of building is learning that a site is one object seen from different angles, not a sequence of surprises. Constraint made this look expensive. Not effort. Full prompt goes in the Academy soon. Amateurs add a new idea per section. Studios reshape one. How many ideas does your last site have ? Save this if you want sites that feel whole 🌌 #lovablepartner #buildinpublic #webdesign #webgl #fyp

caption: How I build with Claude 👇 Academy in bio 🔗 12 months of knowledge made this site. The build took one morning. This studio wanted online booking. Every tutorial says database, accounts, a booking SaaS at 40 a month. I built none of it. Steal this for free: Stop asking what the feature does. Ask where it has to end. Turn photos into drawings: filter: grayscale(1) contrast(1.6), then mix-blend-mode: multiply over an off-white #F4F2ED background. The white of the image disappears and it reads as ink on paper 2. Blueprint grid: repeating-linear-gradient in both directions, 1px lines at rgba(0,0,0,.06), 40px apart, on a fixed background layer 3. Corner crosshairs: a small + drawn with two 1px pseudo elements, absolutely placed at each corner of the frame. This one detail sells the whole thing 4. Hairlines only: 1px borders, never rounded, and ONE accent color used at 5% of the page 5. Numbers in font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums so figures line up like a spec sheet Save this if you build for studios 📐 #[tool tag] #buildinpublic #webdesign #minimal #fyp

author: 0xtommythomas
caption: For 20 years, SaaS companies got rich charging per user. You paid $30 a month whether your team logged in or not. AI agents are breaking that entire model. When one agent does the job of 5 people, companies don't need 5 seats anymore. They need 1. If software companies keep charging per user, their customers pay them 80% less. That is why software is rapidly shifting from SaaS to RaaS: Results as a Service. Instead of paying a monthly subscription for dashboard access, you only pay for completed outcomes: - Intercom Fin charges 99¢ only when the AI resolves a ticket. - AI sales agents charge per booked meeting, not per login. If you are building software or vibe coding apps today, charging per seat is already a dead end. Would you pay for access, or pay for results? author: asmaldigital
caption: Business owner, if you think vibe coding means you can build your own software and cancel the tools you pay for, the front end is the easy part. Everyone says SaaS is going to be dead. Vibe coding is going to take over everything. I don't think so. So will vibe coding kill SaaS in 2026? My view: no. Because there's so much that goes into real software. Here's where vibe coding works: - Building a prototype - Building something for yourself - Building something for internal purposes That's great. But even for that, you still need skills. It's not like anybody can just open Claude Code and start building something that holds up. Here's what vibe coding doesn't solve for you: 1. The back end. You'll be able to build the front end. The back end is going to be a problem. 2. Maintenance. That's going to be a problem too. 3. Connection to other tools. Your software has to work with the rest of your business. 4. Security. In my view, this is the most important one. Security is becoming a big issue now. Thinking about building your own app with AI? Ask yourself four questions first. Step 1: Can I build the back end, not just the front end? Step 2: Who is going to maintain it? Step 3: How will it connect to my other tools? Step 4: How will I keep it secure? Vibe coding is a great start. It just isn't the whole job. Learn to build with AI properly, with the skills that go past the prototype. Join me at aileadbuilder.com #vibecoding #aicoding #saas #claudecode #aiforbusiness

author: erikfisherofficial
caption: The demo went great. So why did the deal die? If you sell for an AI startup, the playbook is simple: get them to the demo, let the tool sell itself. And at small companies, it works. At a big company, the people on your demo are at the bottom of the stream. Above them sit the business priority, the budget your tool is fighting for, the bigger vendor they already pay, plus security, procurement and vendor risk. You're not losing to a better product. You're losing to everything upstream you never found out about. Work upstream before you ever demo: 1. Find the business priority and who's on the hook for it 2. Find the money and what else is fighting for it 3. Map the path to signature (almost no rep does this one) I've sold over $200M in 20 years, and this is the most common reason I see enterprise deals stall. DM me UNICORN and I'll send you the exact questions I ask before I ever give a demo. #b2bsales #enterprisesales #aistartups #saas #salestips

author: nate.b.jones
caption: AI Engineer Devin at Work Every engineering team has tasks that keep getting pushed down the backlog—those annoying frontend bugs, tricky refactors, or features that are important but not urgent. That’s where Devin, an AI-powered software engineer, comes in. Devin isn’t here to replace developers. It’s built to handle the tasks nobody has time for, keeping your team focused on the high-impact work only humans can do. Here’s how Devin helps: 	•	Fixing Forgotten Bugs: Tag Devin in Slack when a small bug slips through the cracks. It tracks down the problem and submits a pull request—all without interrupting your flow. 	•	Drafting Overdue Features: Got a backlog item that’s been gathering dust? Assign it to Devin, and it’ll create an initial pull request so you can refine, not start from scratch. 	•	Cleaning Up Code: Use the VSCode extension to ask Devin for code refactors when things get messy. It handles the repetitive cleanup so your team can focus on tougher problems. Devin learns through your feedback, improving with every task. The more specific you are about what you need, the better its code gets. It’s already helped real teams by fixing bugs and adding features to: 	•	Google’s Go GitHub Client – Improved how HTTP errors are handled. 	•	Anthropic’s MCP Project – Solved browser bugs in cutting-edge AI tools. 	•	Karpathy’s nanoGPT & Llama Index – Improved AI research projects through new features and bug fixes. Devin isn’t a silver bullet—but it’s a real tool that tackles the jobs no one had time to do before. Think of it as a helpful, tireless teammate that frees your engineers to focus on what matters most. #Devin #AI #Engineering #Engineer #Tech #Career #Job #Jobs #TechTrends #Startup #Coding #Code #Dev #CareerAdvice #Mentor #Mentorship #MentorTikTok #CareerTok #JobAdvice #JobTips #Hack #Hacks #Tips #ProductManager #ProductManagement #Business #OpenAI #Microsoft #Google #Gemini #Anthropic #Claude #Llama #Meta #Nvidia #2024 #Future #Story #Sales #Marketing #Agent #Workflow #Smart #Thinking #Strategy #Cool #Real #TechTok #OpenAIDevDay #AIUpdates #VoiceAI #DeveloperLife #Cursor #Replit #Pythagora #Bolt

author: legitalgorithmswithpeter
caption: 🤯 Your computer can’t calculate 0.1 + 0.2 correctly. And a similar rounding error once contributed to the deaths of 28 soldiers. Here’s why. 💻 Computers store numbers in binary, not decimal. Just like 1/3 becomes 0.3333… forever, numbers like 0.1 have repeating binary representations. IEEE 754 floating-point numbers have limited precision, so the computer stores the closest representable value instead. That’s why in languages like Python and JavaScript: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 😳 Usually harmless. But tiny errors can become dangerous when they accumulate over time. 🚨 In 1991, a Patriot missile system in Saudi Arabia suffered a timing error after running for around 100 hours. The accumulated drift contributed to its failure to track an incoming Scud missile. The missile struck a barracks, killing 28 soldiers. 🔥 How developers avoid these problems: ✅ Use integers for money, such as cents. ✅ Use exact decimal types when appropriate, like Java’s BigDecimal or Python’s Decimal. ✅ Compare floating-point numbers using a tolerance instead of exact equality. One tiny rounding error can teach a massive lesson about software engineering. 💬 Want to learn how banks handle precision in financial systems? Comment below! #Programming #FloatingPoint #SoftwareEngineering #ComputerScience #Coding

author: alvin.the.programmer
caption: Most software engineers know that the first example has a linear O(n) space complexity due to the space consumed on the call stack, but far less know the space complexity of the second example. 🧠 ANSWER: O(n) That's right. The second example ALSO has an O(n) space complexity. Although the second example has two recursive calls in it, the space consumed on the call stack remains the same.  How could this be? Since the second example makes more recursive calls, shouldn't it consume more stack space? Nope.  The key is that the maximum stack depth is the same for both. The first example forms a recursive chain like: 2 | 1 | 0 The second example forms a recursive tree like: ⠀⠀⠀2 ⠀⠀/⠀⠀\ ⠀1⠀⠀⠀1 ⠀/ \⠀⠀ / \ 0⠀0⠀ 0⠀0 The depth of both of these structures is identical. 🚨👀 For a fully animated explanation of how the call stack works go to my page and watch reel titled "EP 6 Call Stack & Space Complexity DSA Explained"  #coding #leetcode #softwareengineer #computerscience #softwareengineering [software engineer, leetcode, coding, computer science, software engineering, cs major, data structures and algorithms]

author: alanonai
caption: People ask me all the time how I code with AI. Here's the short answer. I use Claude Code. But the code is the AI's job. My job is the decisions. And I keep three habits on every app I build, even the little ones I make for myself on a Saturday. One. Know which decisions are yours. Before it builds anything, ask the AI what has to be decided first. Read the list. Answer the ones that matter to you. Two. Read what you build on. Whatever it hands you before it starts building, read it. Actually read it. A wrong sentence is one sentence to fix before it's built, and a lot more after. Three. Verify, don't ask. If your app has logins, or anyone's information but your own, check it yourself. Log in as the wrong person and try. A confident yes from the AI that built it proves nothing. That's the floor. Everything else depends on one question. What happens if it's wrong? If it's just for you, those three habits are plenty. If clients are logging in with private files, you want a lot more. That's the short version. The long version is a sixteen-part series, and this is the last one. Series is called Build with AI. This article is "How Much of This Do You Actually Need?" Link's in comments. #ai #vibecoding #programming #coding

author: wolframoviy02
caption: #мем #programming #it #programminghumor #истории  «Пэтриот» (англ. Patriot, с англ. — «патриот», войсковой индекс — MIM-104) — американский зенитный ракетный комплекс большого радиуса действия, состоящий на вооружении Армии США и армий ряда других стран. Производится группой американских компаний во главе с «Рэйтеон». Комплекс «Пэтриот» создавался для замены зенитно-ракетных комплексов «Найк Геркулес» и «Хок» в качестве универсального средства противовоздушной обороны позиционных районов войск на средних и больших высотах. Помимо этого, Patriot должен был обеспечивать противоракетную оборону (ПРО) на уровне армии США. В октябре 1980 года был подписан контракт на производство серийной партии комплексов и ракет, в декабре 1981 года начались поставки в войска. На вооружение принят в 1982 году. Официальное словесное название комплекса является бэкронимом от фразы англ. Phased Array Tracking Radar to Intercept On Target ([комплекс, сопряжённый с] РЛС сопровождения c фазированной антенной решёткой для перехвата цели по линии визирования). В войсках за характерный вид контейнерной пусковой установки комплекс неформально называют «мусоровоз с гидроприводом» (dumpster on hydraulics). В настоящий момент эксплуатируется и поставляется в другие страны усовершенствованная версия системы, «Patriot» PAC-3. Цена поставки 9 батарей (по 4 ПУ на батарею) систем «Пэтриот» может доходить до 9 млрд $ (включает в себя 36 ПУ ЗУР «Пэтриот» PAC-3 (9 батарей по 4 ПУ), 288 ЗУР «Пэтриот» PAC-3, 216 ЗУР с усовершенствованным наведением GEM-T, 10 комплектов РЛС с фазированной решёткой, 10 контрольных станций захвата цели). Стоимость пуска одной ракеты составляет от 3 до 8 млн долл. США в зависимости от типа ракеты.

caption: ⚔️ React vs Next.js — Is Next.js actually a replacement for React? 🤯 No! Next.js is built ON TOP of React. Every Next.js app uses React. Think of React as a car engine. Next.js is the complete car, with everything else you need to drive. 🚗💨 🔥 Here’s what makes them different: ⚛️ React: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces. You choose additional tools for routing, rendering, and other features. 🚀 Next.js: A full React framework with routing, server rendering, static generation, and built-in optimizations. 🌐 SEO & Performance: Next.js supports multiple rendering strategies to help deliver content faster and improve search visibility. 🗂️ Routing: React typically needs a separate routing library. Next.js uses file-based routing. 🖥️ Backend: Next.js supports server-side logic and API endpoints, while React alone focuses on the UI. 🎯 Which should you choose? Use React for interactive dashboards and internal tools. Choose Next.js for blogs, e-commerce stores, and public websites that benefit from SEO and server rendering. 💡 The bottom line: Learn React first. author: wolframoviy02
caption: возвращение деда #программирование #программист #programming #python #мем  Цикл for — это управляющая конструкция в программировании, которая повторяет блок кода заданное количество раз или перебирает элементы коллекции. Используется, когда известна точная длина или количество итераций. Состоит из трех частей в круглых скобках: Инициализация: создание и настройка счетчика (выполняется один раз). Условие: проверка перед каждым шагом; если истинно (true), код выполняется. Шаг (инкремент/декремент): изменение счетчика после каждого прохода. В Python цикл for работает как итератор — он по очереди перебирает элементы любого итерабельного объекта (списка, строки, диапазона). break: полностью прерывает и завершает работу цикла досрочно. continue: пропускает текущий шаг и сразу переходит к следующей итерации.

author: rick.theengineer
caption: Why didn't we just invent ONE programming language and use it for everything? 🤔 Everything in this video is real output. I ran it all on an actual computer 👇 💾 1950s: the quadratic formula as machine code is 49 numbers. Then FORTRAN let scientists write it in ONE line, the way they'd write it on paper. 🏦 1959: COBOL was built for business records: banks, payroll, accounting. Already two languages, two completely different problems. ⚙️ 1972: C gave programmers raw control over memory… and the power to crash. Overflow an 8-byte buffer and the program jumps to address 0x4141414141414141. That's the letter "A", typed by the user. That's how programs get hacked. ☕ Java promised "write once, run anywhere" and cleaned up memory automatically. 🐍 Python bet on simplicity: 8 lines of Java become 1 line of Python… but on the same loop, Python took 3.886 s while C took 0.032 s. That's 121× slower. 🦀 Rust refuses to compile memory bugs at all. The program never even runs, yet it's almost as fast as C. So why not combine everything into one perfect language? Because every design choice is a trade-off: control vs safety, simplicity vs power, automatic memory vs maximum speed. You can't max both ends of the same slider. Languages didn't multiply because engineers couldn't agree on syntax. They multiplied because computing kept creating new problems 🔁 Which language did you learn first, and which one do you actually use today? Tell me below 👇 Save this for the next time someone asks "which language should I learn?" 📌 #programming #coding #computerscience #softwareengineering #techhistory

author: machinelearningtogo
caption: ➡️ Part 1 of Machine Learning & AI simply explained Concepts, no code: what AI is, what machine learning adds, and how the two fit together. Two questions guide the video: what even is AI, and what makes machine learning different? Step 1, AI. Short for artificial intelligence, AI is a big goal: computers that do things we would call smart, like playing chess, understanding speech or driving a car. Step 2, rules by hand. For decades, people built AI by writing every rule themselves. If this happens, then do that. That works for a game like chess. It falls apart for spotting a cat in a photo, because no list of rules covers a cat hiding behind a sofa. Step 3, machine learning. Machine learning builds AI from examples. You show the computer thousands of pictures, each labeled cat or not cat, and it works out the rules by itself. Step 4, how they fit together. AI is the goal, and machine learning is one way to reach it, the way that learns from data. Inside machine learning sits deep learning, which uses neural networks with many layers. Inside deep learning sit chatbots like ChatGPT, large language models trained on huge amounts of text. Step 5, why they get mixed up. Almost every AI in the news today uses machine learning, so people treat the two words like one. A chess program built only from hand-written rules is still AI, with no learning inside at all. The short answers. What is AI? The big goal of machines doing smart things. What is machine learning? The part of AI that finds its own rules in examples. Every machine learning system is AI. Some AI never learns anything. #machinelearning #ai #neuralnetworks #chatgpt #computerscience

author: dopaminedevs
caption: The expensive part of AI code was never writing it. It's reading it, reviewing it and owning it for years. Ponytail (a Claude Code plugin by DietrichGebert) is built on that idea: every line an agent adds is a line you now maintain, so the best diff is often the smallest one. Ask for a date picker and a default agent writes 335 lines. Ponytail writes 10. Version 5 pushes it further. A review command that finds what the diff hides, an audit that ranks the whole repo by what to fix first, and a live band for cost, tokens and tests (Claude Code only). The headline numbers, 53% less code, 41% less time, 98% of risky logic tested, are the project's own, from 39 tasks. Not an independent benchmark. Worth testing on your own repo before you trust them. Install: /plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail, then /plugin install ponytail@ponytail When your agent can write anything, is restraint the skill you want it to have? Repo: github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail  #claudecode #aicoding #vibecoding #opensource #devtools

author: mqwerjust
caption: What is Claude Opus 5.5? 🤖 Claude Opus 5.5 is the latest flagship AI model from Anthropic, the company behind Claude. "Opus" is Anthropic's top tier of publicly available models, built for the hardest tasks: complex reasoning, coding, research, analysis and long multi-step work. How the Claude lineup works: • Haiku is the fastest and lightest, for quick simple tasks • Sonnet is the balanced everyday model • Opus is the most powerful public tier, for complex challenges • Mythos is Anthropic's newest tier above Opus, currently limited to select partners What "5.5" means: It's the version number. Every new generation gets smarter at reasoning, coding and following long instructions. 5.5 is a step up within the 5th generation. author: ballaranigianluigi
caption: Claude Opus 4.8: Anthropic lancia l’AI che coordina centinaia di agenti autonomi Anthropic ha appena presentato Claude Opus 4.8 e la parte più importante non sono i benchmark. La vera rivoluzione sono i “dynamic workflows”: sistemi in cui l’intelligenza artificiale crea da sola un piano operativo, coordina sub-agent, verifica risultati, corregge errori e lavora in parallelo su task enormi. In pratica: un’AI che organizza altre AI. Ed è qui che cambia tutto. Per anni abbiamo usato chatbot. Ora iniziano ad apparire sistemi che si comportano più come organizzazioni operative autonome che come semplici assistenti. Nel video pubblicato da Anthropic si vedono anche i team interni che cercano di “rompere” il modello prima del rilascio, stressandolo e spingendolo al limite. Perché il problema non è più soltanto: “quanto è intelligente?” Ma: “cosa succede quando coordina centinaia di processi contemporaneamente?” #Claude #Anthropic #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #ClaudeOpus Opus48 Tech Future AIagents Automation MachineLearning AGI Startup Technology Innovation

author: room.of.ceo
caption: @Slash  CEO Victor Cardenas Codriansky is a Venezuelan entrepreneur and fintech founder best known as the co-founder of Slash, a venture-backed financial platform designed for modern startups and online companies. He is also a recipient of the Thiel Fellowship, a prestigious program that supports young founders building ambitious companies. Cardenas was born and raised in Caracas, Venezuela, a country that has faced major economic instability and hyperinflation over the past two decades. Growing up in such an environment shaped his interest in financial systems and the importance of reliable banking infrastructure. Experiencing how unstable currency and financial systems affect everyday life motivated him to explore how technology could improve global financial services. He later moved to the United States to study computer science at Stanford University. While studying there, he became deeply involved in the Silicon Valley startup ecosystem and began building technology products focused on financial services. One of his early projects was a fintech tool designed to help people manage and split shared expenses digitally. Cardenas eventually left Stanford after being selected as a Thiel Fellow, choosing to focus entirely on entrepreneurship. He later co-founded Slash, which aims to provide modern financial infrastructure for startups, online businesses, and creators. The platform offers services such as business banking tools, payment systems, and financial management features tailored to companies operating in the digital economy. Produced by: @AtomikGrowth  #finance #money #entrepreneur #billionaire #moneymindset #success #business #ceo #founder #startup
